text: API Gateway Sources: AWS API Gateway Developer Guide, Kong Gateway documentation What it is: A single entry point that sits in front of a collection of backend services (especially in a microservices architecture) and routes each incoming request to the right service. Clients talk to one gateway instead of knowing about every individual service's address. What it handles (so individual services don't have to): Routing: maps a path/method to the right backend service (/users → user-service, /orders → order-service). Authentication: validates JWT/API keys once at the edge, so downstream services trust the gateway instead of each re-implementing auth. Rate limiting: throttles per-client request rate before it ever reaches backend services, protecting them from being overwhelmed. Request/response transformation: e.g. converting a legacy SOAP backend response to JSON for modern clients, without changing the backend. Aggregation: combining calls to multiple services into a single client-facing response (sometimes called the "backend for frontend" pattern) — a mobile app screen might need data from 3 services, gateway can fan out and merge. Observability: single place to log, trace, and monitor all API traffic instead of instrumenting every service separately. TLS termination: gateway handles HTTPS, internal traffic between gateway and services can be plain HTTP within a trusted network. Gateway vs Load Balancer: A load balancer (L4/L7) distributes traffic across replicas of the *same* service based on IP/path. An API gateway routes across *different* services and adds application-level concerns (auth, rate limiting, transformation) on top — they're often used together: gateway routes to a service name, load balancer distributes across that service's replicas. Failure mode to watch for: Single point of failure — if the gateway goes down, every service behind it is unreachable even if they're all healthy. Mitigated by running multiple gateway instances behind their own load balancer, and keeping the gateway itself stateless so any instance can handle any request. Backend for Frontend (BFF) pattern: Instead of one generic gateway for all clients, run a dedicated gateway per client type (mobile-BFF, web-BFF) — each shaped to that client's specific data needs, avoiding a single gateway trying to please every consumer with one generic contract. Real-world example: A ride-sharing app's mobile client hits a single gateway endpoint. Gateway validates the JWT, then calls trip-service, pricing-service, and driver-location-service in parallel, merges their responses into one JSON payload the app expects — the mobile client never needs to know these are three separate backend services, or that pricing-service might be redeployed independently tomorrow.

text: Rate Limiter System Design Sources: Stripe API documentation (Rate Limiters), Cloudflare Learning Center (Rate Limiting) What it is: A rate limiter controls how many requests a client can make in a given time window. Critical for APIs to prevent abuse, ensure fair usage, and protect backend services. Used by every major API: Twitter, Stripe, Razorpay, GitHub. Algorithms: 1. Token Bucket (most common): Each user gets a bucket with N tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens refill at a fixed rate. If bucket empty, request rejected. Allows short bursts (use all tokens at once) but limits sustained rate. Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe. 2. Sliding Window Log: Store timestamp of every request in a sorted set (Redis). On each request, remove timestamps older than window, count remaining. If count >= limit, reject. Accurate but memory-intensive. 3. Fixed Window Counter: Simple counter per user per time window (e.g., per minute). Reset counter at window boundary. Fast and memory efficient. Problem: burst at window boundary (double the rate for a brief moment). 4. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue (bucket). Processed at fixed rate. Smooths out bursts. Good for output rate limiting. Implementation with Redis: Redis is ideal for rate limiting because: - Atomic operations (INCR, EXPIRE) prevent race conditions - Sub-millisecond latency - Distributed — works across multiple API server instances Redis token bucket implementation: INCR user:123:requests EXPIRE user:123:requests 60 If value > limit: reject request Where to implement: - API Gateway layer (before hitting your services) - Middleware in FastAPI/Express - Nginx level for simple cases Distributed Rate Limiting Challenge: With multiple servers, each server has its own counter. text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. Real-world takeaway for interviews: "Design Slack/a chat app" questions hinge on separating three different problems that are easy to conflate: durable message storage (needs to be correct and never lost), real-time fan-out to online clients (needs to be fast, some staleness on reconnect is fine since history backfills it), and ephemeral presence state (needs to be cheap and fast, correctness is optional) — each deserves a different consistency/durability trade-off.

text: Load Balancer System Design Sources: AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation, NGINX documentation (Load Balancing) What it is: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. Prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck. Essential for high availability and horizontal scaling. Types of Load Balancers: 1. Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes based on IP and TCP/UDP port. Fast, no content inspection. Cannot route based on URL path or headers. Example: AWS Network Load Balancer. 2. Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes based on HTTP content — URL, headers, cookies. Can do path-based routing (/api → API servers, /static → CDN). Example: AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx. Load Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin: Requests distributed evenly in order. Simple, works well when servers have equal capacity. Weighted Round Robin: Servers get requests proportional to weight. Used when servers have different capacities. Least Connections: New request goes to server with fewest active connections. Better for long-lived connections (WebSockets, streaming). IP Hash: Client IP hashed to always hit same server. Useful for session stickiness (user always hits same server). Problem: uneven distribution if many users share an IP (NAT). Consistent Hashing: Used for distributed cache and storage routing. Minimizes remapping when servers are added or removed. Health Checks: Load balancer pings each server every few seconds. If server fails health check, removed from rotation automatically. When server recovers, added back automatically. This is how zero-downtime deployments work. Session Stickiness (Sticky Sessions): Problem: User login session stored on Server A. Request goes to Server B — user logged out. Solution 1: Sticky sessions — same user always hits same server (IP hash). Solution 2: Externalize sessions to Redis — any server can read any session. Solution 2 is better for true stateless servers. Real-world stack for Swiggy scale: DNS → AWS Route53 (global traffic routing) → AWS CloudFront (CDN + DDoS protection) → AWS ALB (Layer 7, path-based routing) → Auto Scaling Groups (EC2 instances) → Services

An index is a separate data structure that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, typically O(log n), at the cost of extra storage and slower writes (the index must be updated on every insert/update/delete too). B-Tree index (the default, general-purpose case): Balanced tree structure, keeps data sorted, supports equality (=) and range (<, >, BETWEEN) queries efficiently, and supports ORDER BY without an extra sort step if the sort matches the index order. This is what you get by default when you index a column in Postgres/MySQL. Hash index: Only supports exact-match equality lookups (=), not ranges. Faster than B-Tree for pure equality lookups in principle, but rarely used in practice because B-Tree covers equality well enough and also handles ranges — using a hash index means giving up range queries for a marginal equality speedup. Composite (multi-column) indexes and column order: An index on (user_id, created_at) can efficiently serve queries filtering on user_id alone, or user_id + created_at together — but NOT an efficient query on created_at alone, because the index is sorted by user_id first. Rule of thumb: put the column used for equality filters first, range/sort columns after — column order in a composite index is not arbitrary. text: Bloom Filters Sources: Burton H. Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Amazon Dynamo (Case Study) Sources: DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) Why it was built: Amazon's shopping cart service needed to always accept a write — even during a network partition or node failure — because a customer being unable to add to their cart is a direct lost sale. Traditional strongly-consistent databases prioritize consistency over availability during a partition; Dynamo inverted that priority for this specific use case. Core design goal: always writable. Dynamo chose availability and partition tolerance over strict consistency (the AP side of CAP) — a write should never be rejected because some replicas are temporarily unreachable. This means the system can end up with temporarily conflicting versions of the same data, which it must reconcile later rather than prevent up front. Consistent hashing for partitioning: Data is partitioned across nodes using consistent hashing (each node owns a range on a hash ring). Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the data immediately adjacent to it on the ring, not the entire dataset — critical for a system meant to scale nodes up/down without a massive rebalancing event. Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff: Normally a write requires acknowledgment from W replicas and a read from R replicas (with W + R > N giving strong-ish consistency). But if some of the "correct" replica nodes are down, Dynamo still accepts the write on a different, temporarily-substituting node ("sloppy quorum") rather than rejecting it — the substitute node holds a "hint" to hand the data back to the rightful replica once it recovers (hinted handoff). This is the core mechanism of the "always writable" guarantee. Vector clocks for conflict resolution: Because writes can be accepted by different replicas independently during a partition, the same key can end up with multiple conflicting versions. Dynamo tags each version with a vector clock (tracks which node made which update, in what order) so it can determine if one version is a strict descendant of another (safe to auto-merge) or if they're genuinely concurrent conflicting writes (must be reconciled — Dynamo pushes this reconciliation to the application, e.g. "merge the two shopping carts," since only the application knows how to correctly merge domain data). Read-repair & anti-entropy: When a read encounters divergent versions across replicas, the coordinator can push the resolved/latest version back to the stale replicas ("read repair") instead of waiting for a separate background process — keeps replicas converging toward consistency without blocking writes to do so. Legacy and influence: Dynamo's design (consistent hashing, eventual consistency, vector clocks, "AP over CP" for write availability) directly influenced Cassandra, Riak, and Amazon's own managed DynamoDB — this paper is one of the most cited references in distributed systems design precisely because it made an explicit, well-justified trade-off (availability over consistency) that became a standard pattern to reference when discussing CAP theorem trade-offs in interviews.

Bloom, "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" (1970), Redis documentation (Bloom Filter / probabilistic data structures) What it is: A probabilistic data structure that answers "have I possibly seen this item before?" using a fixed, tiny amount of memory — regardless of how many items have been added. Trades perfect accuracy for massive space savings. The guarantee (this is the important part): No false negatives: if the filter says "definitely not present," the item is genuinely not present. Possible false positives: if the filter says "possibly present," it might actually not be — the false positive rate is tunable (smaller filter / more items = higher false positive rate). It never says "definitely present" for something that was never added incorrectly in the wrong direction — the asymmetry only goes one way, which is what makes it usable: you only need a secondary, slower check for the "possibly present" case. How it works: A bit array of m bits, all initially 0, plus k independent hash functions. To add an item: hash it k times, set the k resulting bit positions to 1. To check an item: hash it the same k times, if ALL k bit positions are 1, report "possibly present"; if ANY bit is 0, report "definitely not present" (since adding that item would have set that bit). False positives happen because bits get shared/overwritten by other items' hashes — you can't tell whether a set bit was set by the item you're checking or by pure coincidence from other insertions. Why not just use a hash set: A hash set storing millions of actual keys uses far more memory (must store each key or at least its full hash) than a Bloom filter, which only needs a handful of bits per item regardless of key size. The trade is: a hash set has zero false positives, a Bloom filter accepts a small false-positive rate in exchange for a fraction of the memory. Cannot remove items (in the basic version): Because bits are shared across multiple items' hashes, clearing a bit to "remove" one item could break the correctness for other items that also set that bit. A Counting Bloom Filter (using small counters instead of single bits) supports removal at the cost of more memory — used when deletions are actually needed. Real-world example: A CDN or database wants to avoid an expensive disk/network lookup for keys that definitely don't exist (e.g. checking if a URL is on a known-malicious list, or if a cache key might exist before hitting disk). Check the Bloom filter first: if "definitely not present," skip the expensive lookup entirely. If "possibly present," do the real (slower, authoritative) lookup to confirm — the small false-positive rate just means occasionally doing an unnecessary real lookup, never missing an item that's actually there. text: Distributed Locks & Leader Election Sources: Redis documentation (Distributed Locks with Redis / Redlock), Apache ZooKeeper documentation, etcd documentation What it is: A distributed lock lets multiple processes across different machines coordinate so only one of them does a particular piece of work at a time — e.g. only one instance of a cron job runs, or only one node processes a given task. A regular in-process lock (mutex) doesn't work here because the "processes" are on different machines with no shared memory. Why you need one: Running the same scheduled job twice (duplicate emails sent, duplicate charges). Two nodes both thinking they're the "leader" and both writing conflicting data. Preventing two workers from picking up and processing the same queue item. Redis-based locks (simple case): SET a key with a unique value and an expiry (SET lock_key unique_id NX EX 30). NX means "only set if not exists" — this is the actual locking mechanism. Expiry (EX) prevents a deadlock if the holder crashes before releasing. Release by checking the value matches before deleting (via a Lua script, to make compare-and-delete atomic) — otherwise you might delete a lock some other process acquired after your expiry. Limitation: single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it fails over to a replica before the write is replicated, two clients could both believe they hold the lock. Redlock (multi-node Redis locking): Acquire the lock on a majority of independent Redis nodes (e.g. 3 of 5) within a time budget. Considered "acquired" only if majority succeeds before the clock runs out. More resilient to a single node failing, though it has been debated (Martin Kleppmann's critique) as not being fully safe under clock drift/GC pauses — good enough for "efficiency" locks (avoid duplicate work), not for correctness-critical locks (avoid data corruption). ZooKeeper / etcd-based locks (correctness-critical case): Both are consensus-based stores (using ZAB / Raft respectively) — a write is only acknowledged once a majority of nodes agree, which is much stronger than a single Redis node's guarantee. Leader election pattern: each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential node; the candidate with the lowest sequence number is the leader. If the leader's session dies (crash, network partition), its ephemeral node disappears automatically and the next-lowest candidate becomes leader. Use this when correctness matters more than latency — e.g. only one node should ever be allowed to write to a given shard. Fencing tokens: Even with a "correct" lock, a paused process (GC pause, slow disk) can wake up after its lock has expired and still think it holds the lock, then write stale data. Fix: every time a lock is granted, issue a monotonically increasing fencing token. The resource being protected (e.g. storage service) rejects any write that comes with an older token than the last one it saw — this is the actual fix for "lock expired but process is still running" bugs, the lock alone is not sufficient. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Database Replication & Failover Sources: PostgreSQL documentation (Replication), MySQL documentation (Replication), "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.5 What it is: Replication keeps copies of the same data on multiple database nodes. Goals: survive a node failure without data loss, serve more read traffic than one machine can handle, and keep data closer to users in different regions. Leader-follower (primary-replica) replication: One node (leader) accepts all writes. Writes are streamed to one or more followers, which apply them and can serve read traffic. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Dead-letter queues (DLQ): Messages that fail processing repeatedly (e.g. 5 retries) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue forever. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Real-world example: E-commerce checkout: "order placed" event published to a topic. → Inventory service subscribes, decrements stock. → Billing service subscribes, charges card. → Notification service subscribes, sends confirmation email. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - text: LinkedIn & the Origin of Kafka (Case Study) Sources: LinkedIn Engineering Blog, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) The problem LinkedIn had: By the early 2010s, LinkedIn had many separate systems that needed the same underlying activity data — the news feed, search indexing, relevance/ML pipelines, monitoring, and analytics all needed a feed of user activity events (page views, connections made, likes). Each consumer had built its own point-to-point pipeline to get this data, resulting in an N×M mess of custom, fragile integrations between every producer and every consumer. Why existing message queues weren't a fit: Traditional queues (JMS-style brokers) were built for low-throughput, transactional messaging, not the sustained high-throughput firehose of activity events LinkedIn needed to move (hundreds of billions of events/day at LinkedIn's later scale). They also typically delete a message once consumed, so a second, independent consumer couldn't replay the same stream. Kafka's core design choices (as a direct response to that problem): Log-based storage: instead of deleting messages after delivery, Kafka retains them for a configured period (or forever) as an append-only log. Multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream at their own pace, tracking their own offset — this single change is what let LinkedIn support many different downstream consumers off one shared pipeline instead of N separate point-to-point integrations. Partitioning: each topic is split into partitions, each handled independently and in order, allowing horizontal scaling of both writes and reads by adding more partitions and consumers. Sequential disk I/O: Kafka relies on sequential reads/writes to disk (fast, even on spinning disks) plus OS page cache, rather than random access — this is why Kafka achieves very high throughput despite persisting everything. Pull-based consumption: consumers pull at their own pace and track their own offset, rather than the broker pushing and needing to track per-consumer state — simplifies the broker and lets slow consumers fall behind without overwhelming themselves, catching up later from their last offset. Outcome: LinkedIn open-sourced Kafka in 2011 and it became an Apache project; it's now the de facto standard for high-throughput event streaming across the industry (adopted by Netflix, Uber, and most large-scale systems that need a durable, replayable, multi-consumer event backbone) — a direct example of solving an internal integration problem generally enough that it became foundational infrastructure well beyond its original use case. Relevance to system design interviews: "Why Kafka over a traditional queue" is a common follow-up question — the answer is precisely this history: replayability (log retention, multiple independent consumer groups) and throughput (partitioning + sequential I/O), not just "it's a queue but faster."

text: Message Queues & Pub-Sub Sources: AWS SQS Developer Guide, RabbitMQ documentation, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.11 What it is: A message queue decouples producers (services that create work) from consumers (services that process it). Producer pushes a message, queue holds it, consumer pulls and processes it whenever ready. Neither side needs the other to be online at the same instant. Why use one: Smooths traffic spikes — queue absorbs a burst, consumers drain it at their own pace. Decouples services — producer doesn't care if consumer is slow, down, or scaled to zero. Enables retries — failed messages can be redelivered instead of lost. Enables async workflows — user gets a fast response, heavy work happens in background (e.g. "order placed" returns instantly, email/invoice generation happens after). Point-to-point vs Pub/Sub: Point-to-point (queue): one message, one consumer. Used for task distribution — e.g. a pool of workers pulling image-resize jobs off a queue. Pub/Sub (topic): one message, many subscribers. Used for fan-out — e.g. "order placed" event notifies inventory service, billing service, and analytics service simultaneously. Delivery guarantees: At-most-once: message may be lost, never duplicated. Fastest, least safe. At-least-once: message guaranteed delivered, but may be duplicated on retry. Most systems (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka) default to this — consumers must be idempotent. Exactly-once: hardest to guarantee in a distributed system; usually achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers (dedupe by message ID), not by the queue itself. Visibility timeout / ack: Consumer pulls a message; queue hides it from other consumers for a timeout window. Consumer processes it, then explicitly acknowledges (deletes) the message. If consumer crashes before ack, message becomes visible again and another consumer picks it up — this is why consumers must be idempotent, since a message could be processed twice. Lets you inspect and reprocess poison messages without stalling healthy traffic. Queue vs Kafka: Traditional queues (SQS, RabbitMQ) delete a message once consumed — it's gone. Kafka is a log: messages are retained for a configured period and consumers track their own offset, so multiple consumer groups can replay the same stream independently. Use a queue for simple task distribution; use Kafka when you need replay, ordering within a partition, or multiple independent consumers of the same event stream. Each subscriber processes independently; if the email service is down, the order still completes — the message just waits in that service's queue until it recovers.

text: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga Pattern Sources: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (Kleppmann) ch.9, microservices.io (Chris Richardson) — "Saga pattern" The problem: A single database transaction (BEGIN...COMMIT) guarantees all-or-nothing across tables in one database. But a "place order" flow in a microservices system might need to update order-service's DB, decrement inventory-service's DB, and charge payment-service's DB — three separate databases, no single transaction can span all of them. Two-Phase Commit (2PC): A coordinator asks every participant to "prepare" (lock resources, confirm it *can* commit, but don't commit yet). If all participants vote yes, coordinator tells everyone to commit. If any vote no, coordinator tells everyone to abort. Guarantees atomicity across multiple resources — either all commit or all abort. Why 2PC is avoided in practice at scale: Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants have "prepared" but before sending commit/abort, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely, waiting for a coordinator that may never come back. Latency: every participant must stay locked and waiting through two full round-trips before any of them can proceed — slow, and doesn't scale well across services owned by different teams with independent uptime. Tight coupling: all participants must be available simultaneously; one slow or down service blocks the whole transaction for everyone. Saga pattern (the common alternative in microservices): Break the transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Example: (1) order-service creates order [compensate: cancel order], (2) inventory-service reserves stock [compensate: release stock], (3) payment-service charges card [compensate: refund]. If step 3 fails, the saga runs compensations for steps 2 and 1 in reverse — no single distributed lock is ever held across all three. Choreography vs Orchestration (two ways to coordinate a saga): Choreography: each service publishes an event when its step completes, next service reacts to that event — fully decentralized, no single point of control, but harder to see the overall flow/state of "which step is this order on." Orchestration: a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state — easier to reason about and debug, but the orchestrator becomes a piece of infrastructure every saga depends on. Key trade-off vs 2PC: Sagas give up strict atomicity (there IS a window where inventory is reserved but payment hasn't happened yet — visible partial state) in exchange for no blocking locks held across services and independent service availability. This is why sagas are preferred in practice: partial visibility for a short window is an acceptable trade for not letting one service's outage freeze every other service's transactions. Real-world example: Booking a flight + hotel as one "trip" transaction: reserve flight seat, reserve hotel room, charge card. If the hotel is sold out by the time that step runs, the saga triggers a compensating action to release the flight seat that was already reserved — the user never ends up charged for a trip that couldn't be fully booked, without ever holding a lock

text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. Searching "wireless headphones" fans out to every shard, each returns its best local matches ranked by BM25, coordinator merges and returns the final top 20 — the same pattern used by product search on any major e-commerce site or by Elasticsearch-backed log search internally at a company.

text: Slack System Design (Case Study) Sources: Slack Engineering Blog (slack.engineering) Core challenge: Real-time message delivery to potentially thousands of connected clients per workspace, while keeping full message history durable and searchable, and keeping every client's view of a channel consistent as new messages, edits, and reactions arrive. Real-time delivery via WebSockets: Each connected client holds a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server. When a message is sent, it's written to the durable store first, then fanned out over the open WebSocket connections of every client currently viewing that channel — the WebSocket is for live delivery to already-connected clients, not the system of record; a client reconnecting after being offline fetches missed history from the durable store via a normal API call, not by expecting to replay it from the socket. The "gateway holds connections, backend holds truth" split: Gateway/connection servers are relatively lightweight and mostly hold open sockets and route messages; the actual message data, ordering, and history lives in the backend datastore. This separation lets Slack scale the number of concurrent open connections independently from the storage/query layer — a spike in simultaneous online users stresses connection servers, not necessarily the database. Sharding by workspace/channel: Slack's engineering blog has discussed sharding message storage by team/channel, since most reads and writes for a given message are scoped to one channel — this keeps related data (a channel's message history) together on the same shard, so a typical "load channel history" query hits one shard rather than fanning out across the whole dataset. Historical MySQL scaling (Vitess): Slack has written about outgrowing a single large MySQL setup and adopting Vitess (a MySQL sharding middleware, originally built at YouTube) to shard their relational data horizontally while keeping the MySQL query interface application code already relied on — an example of solving a scaling problem by adding a sharding layer in front of an existing database technology, rather than fully rewriting onto a different database. Presence (online/offline/typing indicators): Presence state changes extremely frequently (far more often than actual messages) and is far less critical to get perfectly right — a "typing..." indicator being a second late or occasionally wrong is a minor UX blemish, not a correctness bug. This makes presence a good candidate for the most relaxed consistency and heaviest batching/throttling in the whole system, illustrating that not every real-time-feeling feature needs the same delivery guarantees as the actual message content. text: Search & Indexing (Inverted Index) Sources: Elasticsearch documentation ("Inverted index"), Apache Lucene documentation What it is: Searching billions of documents for a keyword by scanning each one would be far too slow. Search engines instead build an inverted index ahead of time — a data structure that maps each word to the list of documents containing it — so a search becomes a fast lookup instead of a full scan. Forward index vs inverted index: Forward index: document → list of words it contains (this is the natural way you'd store a document, but useless for "find all docs containing X"). Inverted index: word → list of documents containing it. Flips the mapping so a query for a term is a single lookup, not a scan of every document. Building the index: 1. Tokenization: split text into individual terms ("The quick fox" → ["the", "quick", "fox"]). 2. Normalization: lowercase, remove punctuation, stemming (running → run) so "run", "runs", "running" all match the same index entry. 3. Stop word removal (optional): common words like "the", "is" are often excluded since they match nearly everything and add little search value. 4. For each remaining term, append the document ID (and often position within the document, for phrase search) to that term's posting list. Querying: A search for "quick fox" looks up the posting list for "quick" and for "fox", then intersects them — documents in both lists contain both words. Ranking (which result appears first) typically uses TF-IDF or BM25: term frequency (how often the word appears in this doc) weighted against inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across all docs) — a rare word matching is a stronger signal than a common word matching. Distributed search (how this scales to billions of documents): The full index doesn't fit on one machine. It's split into shards, each holding a subset of documents and its own local inverted index. A query fans out to every shard in parallel, each returns its top-N matches, and a coordinating node merges and re-ranks the combined results — this is exactly how Elasticsearch/Solr scale search across a cluster. Each shard is also typically replicated for both availability and to spread read (query) load across replicas. Real-time-ish updates: New documents don't need a full index rebuild — an update is added as a small new index segment; a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones for query efficiency. This is why "just indexed" documents often show up in search within seconds, not instantly, and why search indexes trade a small delay for much better write throughput. Real-world example: An e-commerce product search: catalog of 50M products is sharded across many nodes. text: Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS Sources: Martin Fowler's blog (martinfowler.com — "CQRS", "Event Sourcing"), Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (CQRS pattern, Event-driven architecture style) What event-driven architecture is: Services communicate by emitting events ("OrderPlaced", "PaymentFailed") to a broker (Kafka, SNS, RabbitMQ) rather than calling each other's APIs directly. Interested services subscribe to the events they care about and react independently. Producer doesn't know or care who's listening. Why use it over direct service-to-service calls: Loose coupling — order-service doesn't need to know inventory-service, billing-service, and analytics-service exist; it just publishes "OrderPlaced". Adding a new consumer (e.g. a new fraud-detection service) requires zero changes to the producer. Resilience — if notification-service is down, the event waits in its queue; order-service isn't blocked waiting on a slow downstream call. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): Split the model used for writes (commands) from the model used for reads (queries) — instead of one model trying to serve both efficiently. Write side: optimized for validating and persisting a change (e.g. normalized relational tables, enforcing invariants). Read side: optimized for how the data is actually queried (e.g. a denormalized, pre-joined view tailored to a specific screen). The two are kept in sync via events — write side publishes an event on every change, read side subscribes and updates its own denormalized copy. Why CQRS pairs with event-driven design: The event stream that keeps read models in sync *is* the event-driven mechanism — a write triggers an event, one or more read models rebuild themselves from it, independently and asynchronously. Trade-off: eventual consistency. Because the read model updates asynchronously after the write event, there's a window where a query might return stale data (read model hasn't caught up yet). This is fine for a lot of use cases (a "likes count" being one event behind is not a problem) but wrong for anything requiring strict consistency (reading your own bank balance right after a transfer). Event Sourcing (often paired with CQRS, but a separate concept): Instead of storing current state and overwriting it, store the full sequence of events that led to the current state ("AccountOpened", "Deposited $100", "Withdrew $30"). Current state is derived by replaying events. Benefit: full audit trail for free, and you can rebuild any past state or fix a bug in projection logic by replaying history with corrected logic. Cost: replaying a long event history to get current state is slow without periodic snapshots; more operational complexity than just storing current state. Real-world example: An e-commerce order system publishes "OrderPlaced" on write. A dedicated "OrderSummaryView" read model (denormalized, stored in a fast key-value store) subscribes and updates itself — this is the exact table the "My Orders" page in the app queries, pre-shaped for that screen, entirely separate from the normalized orders/line_items tables used to validate and place the order in the first place.

text: APACHE KAFKA — SYSTEM DESIGN DEEP DIVE Sources: Apache Kafka documentation, Kreps, Narkhede, Rao — "Kafka: a Distributed Messaging System for Log Processing" (NetDB 2011) Overview: Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. Think of it as a highly durable, infinitely scalable message queue where producers write events and consumers read them. It's used in almost every large-scale system: Uber uses it for location updates, LinkedIn (who built Kafka) uses it for activity feeds, Netflix uses it for analytics pipeline. Core Concepts: Event/Message: A piece of data — "user_id: 123 placed order_id: 456 at timestamp: 1234567890" Topic: A named log of events. Like a table in a database. E.g., "order-events" topic Producer: Writes events to a topic Consumer: Reads events from a topic Broker: A Kafka server that stores events Cluster: Multiple brokers working together Partition: A topic is split into partitions for parallelism Offset: A sequential ID for each event in a partition (like array index) Consumer Group: Multiple consumers sharing the work of reading a topic Why Kafka? (vs Traditional Message Queues like RabbitMQ): Traditional queue: event consumed → deleted from queue Kafka: events retained for configurable period (default 7 days) → multiple consumers can independently read the same events This is transformative: - Add a new consumer without affecting existing ones - Replay events from past (debugging, backfilling new systems) - Decouple producers from consumers completely Kafka vs RabbitMQ: - RabbitMQ: message broker, push model, messages deleted after consumption, good for task queues - Kafka: event log, pull model, messages retained, good for event streaming and data pipelines - Choose Kafka when: multiple consumers need the same events, need event replay, high throughput - Choose RabbitMQ when: complex routing, guaranteed message ordering per consumer, task-queue pattern Architecture Deep Dive: Topics and Partitions: - Topic "order-events" might have 12 partitions - Each partition is an ordered, immutable log of events - Partitions distributed across brokers (partition 0 on broker 1, partition 1 on broker 2, etc.) - Events within a partition are strictly ordered - Events across partitions have no guaranteed order Partition Key: - Producer specifies a key per event: order.send(key="user_123", value=event) - All events with same key go to same partition - Guarantees ordering for events with same key (e.g., all events for user_123 are ordered) - Without key: round-robin across partitions Replication: - Each partition has a leader and N replicas on different brokers (N = replication factor) - Default replication factor: 3 (1 leader + 2 replicas) - All reads/writes go to leader - Replicas passively sync from leader - If leader fails, a replica is automatically elected as new leader (ZooKeeper or KRaft consensus) - Durability: Kafka can acknowledge write only after all replicas confirm receipt (acks=all) Consumer Groups: - Multiple consumers in a group share partitions - Each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in a group - 12 partitions + 6 consumers = 2 partitions per consumer (parallelism) - 12 partitions + 12 consumers = 1 partition per consumer (max parallelism)

Core components: Seed URLs: the starting set of pages to crawl. Frontier (URL queue): the set of URLs discovered but not yet fetched — this is the main piece of shared state the whole system revolves around. Fetcher: downloads the page content for a URL. Parser/Extractor: pulls new links out of the downloaded HTML, plus whatever content the crawler is actually collecting (text for a search index, prices for a shopping comparison site, etc.). Duplicate detector: avoids re-crawling and re-storing content already seen. Storage: the downloaded content and metadata. Avoiding duplicate work: Two different URLs often point to the same content (mobile vs desktop URL, tracking params, http vs https). Hash the normalized content (not just the URL) to detect "we've already stored this page" even if the URL differs. A Bloom filter is commonly used to cheaply check "have we already queued this URL" before adding it to the frontier, without needing to store every full URL in memory to check. Politeness (this is a hard requirement, not an optimization): Crawling a site too fast can look like — or actually be — a denial-of-service attack, and can get the crawler's IP banned. Rules: respect robots.txt (tells the crawler which paths it's not allowed to fetch), and rate-limit per domain (e.g. max 1 request/second to a given host), typically using a separate queue or delay per domain rather than one global rate limit. Priority / freshness: Not all pages are equal — a news homepage changes hourly, a static about-page almost never. Crawlers assign a re-crawl priority per URL based on how often it has historically changed and how important it is (e.g. via inbound link count, an early precursor to PageRank), rather than crawling everything on a fixed schedule. Scaling the frontier: A single machine's queue can't hold "every URL on the web" and a single fetcher can't download fast enough. The frontier is partitioned (e.g. by domain hash) across many worker machines, each responsible for fetching a subset of URLs — this also naturally helps enforce per-domain politeness, since all URLs for one domain land on the same worker's queue. Handling crawler traps and infinite spaces: Some sites generate infinite URLs dynamically (e.g. a calendar with a "next month" link that goes on forever). Crawlers cap max depth per site and max pages per domain to avoid getting stuck indefinitely on a single site's infinite link structure.
